reference.source: Primer on the Metabolic Bone Diseases and Disorders of Mineral Metabolism (ASBMR)
clinicalPearls: An autosomal recessive sclerosing dysplasia caused by loss-of-function mutations in SOST, which encodes sclerostin
Loss of sclerostin removes a natural brake on Wnt-driven bone formation, producing progressive generalised high bone mass
Characterised by a large mandible, frontal bossing, facial distortion, and tall stature with a heavy skeleton
Syndactyly of the fingers, often with nail dysplasia, is a distinctive associated feature that helps separate it from Van Buchem disease
Skull thickening entraps cranial nerves, so facial-nerve palsy, hearing loss, and optic compromise are characteristic complications
Progressive skull-base overgrowth can raise intracranial pressure and, rarely, cause life-threatening brainstem compression
Management focuses on surgical decompression of entrapped nerves and monitoring for raised intracranial pressure; bisphosphonates are not effective at reducing bone mass
reference.pathophysiology: Sclerosteosis is caused by biallelic inactivating mutations in SOST, the gene encoding sclerostin, a protein secreted by osteocytes that normally inhibits the Wnt/beta-catenin signalling pathway in bone. Without functional sclerostin, Wnt signalling is unrestrained, driving markedly increased osteoblastic bone formation throughout the skeleton. The result is progressive, dense, sclerotic bone with cortical and skull thickening. Overgrowth of the calvaria and skull base narrows cranial foramina, entrapping cranial nerves and, in severe cases, elevating intracranial pressure. The same pathway biology has informed development of anti-sclerostin therapy for osteoporosis.
additionalInvestigations: Plain radiographs showing generalised osteosclerosis, cortical thickening, and calvarial hyperostosis
Cross-sectional skull-base imaging to assess foraminal narrowing and cranial nerve compression
Monitoring for raised intracranial pressure including fundoscopy
Examination for syndactyly and nail changes
redFlags: Signs of raised intracranial pressure such as headache, papilloedema, and vomiting
Progressive facial-nerve palsy or rapidly worsening hearing or vision
Brainstem or cerebellar signs suggesting posterior fossa crowding
Sudden neurological deterioration requiring urgent decompression
reference.prognosis: The disorder is progressive; without intervention, cranial nerve entrapment and raised intracranial pressure can cause serious neurological disability, and severe cases may be life-limiting, though timely surgical decompression can relieve complications.
pitfalls: Confusing sclerosteosis with Van Buchem disease, distinguished by the presence of syndactyly and generally greater severity in sclerosteosis
Attributing progressive facial palsy to idiopathic Bell palsy rather than bony entrapment
Failing to monitor and treat rising intracranial pressure
Expecting antiresorptive drugs to reduce the excess bone mass
references: Primer on the Metabolic Bone Diseases and Disorders of Mineral Metabolism (ASBMR)
GeneReviews / peer-reviewed reviews of SOST-related sclerosing bone dysplasias
management: Undertake timely surgical decompression of narrowed cranial foramina and the skull base to relieve cranial-nerve entrapment and raised intracranial pressure
Manage facial-nerve palsy, hearing loss with hearing aids or implants, and optic compromise supportively
Monitor for raised intracranial pressure with serial fundoscopy and skull-base imaging, intervening before brainstem compression develops
Provide ongoing audiological and visual surveillance with rehabilitation
Avoid anti-sclerostin antibody therapy and other agents that further increase bone mass, since the disorder arises from unrestrained bone formation
Offer genetic counselling and family screening for this autosomal recessive SOST disorder
Refer to a metabolic bone and clinical genetics team, with neurosurgery and ENT input
